dwp_uprating_analysis.title: State Pension uprating analysis 2026
dwp_uprating_analysis.definition: In any given year it will go up by at least inflation or 2.5% – and anything more that is needed to retain that value [the 2029-30 ratio to earnings]
dwp_uprating_analysis.model: Pensim3, DWP's dynamic microsimulation model (population and pension outcomes projected to 2100, ONS 2024-based population projections)
dwp_uprating_analysis.coverage: Great Britain; direct Annually Managed Expenditure, no tax or debt interest effects; rounded to the nearest £1bn; applies a path for uprating (DWP's words), rates not published; HL3774 (15 October 2026): no single-year earnings or prices growth assumptions

method_limitations: Each rise follows the triple lock's convention of September CPI and May-July earnings (the statute requires at least earnings). The central path uses the OBR's September-quarter CPI and April-June earnings for the Aprils 2028-2031 and its calendar-year long-term path after; the monthly model builds both measures from the same simulated months.

The central path follows the OBR's October 2026 Economic and fiscal outlook for calendar years 2026-2030 and the inputs to every April rise to April 2031. Later years follow the OBR's March 2026 long-term economic determinants (dated 28 May 2026), because the OBR published no October 2026 set with that outlook, and the OBR describes its long-term projection as not a forecast. When the OBR publishes the October set, a rebuild replaces every figure for 2031 and later.

The simulated example paths rest on one statistical model of CPI and earnings (a monthly VAR fitted to 2000-2026), shifted so its calendar-year averages equal the OBR's. They show how prices and earnings could move and carry no probability weight: the model failed its frozen statutory screen (C2), so the file makes no probability claim from them.

On policyengine-uk 2.151.0, benefit uprating follows the previous September's CPI (#2557), to 0.1 point and never cut: April 2027 uses the path's September 2026 CPI input and later years the path's September CPI the year before. Additional State Pension follows September CPI.

The population is aged statically: each record represents a person of its age in every year. The Microcosm primary and Enhanced FRS 1.58.2 both anchor in their 2025-26 calibration year: each dataset's own runtime weights are retained through that year and then follow ONS 2024-based age/sex growth. Microcosm's 2025 weights are exactly its solved ones; the Enhanced FRS's are its calibrated ones times 0.9956 (policyengine-uk-data#538). Uncapped ages are retained, including genuine ages of 80; only an entirely top-coded 80+ tail gets represented ages of 80 to 105. State Pension types follow birth cohorts. Deaths, migration and contribution histories are not simulated; pensioners abroad are outside both datasets.
Microcosm records are built from survey donors. The same minimum of ten contributing records and complementary withholding applies to the primary and Enhanced FRS 1.58.2.
Rents and council tax stay at their 2030 amounts after 2030, and dividend, property, savings and self-employment income do not follow the path.

In the survey runs Housing Benefit and council tax reduction respond only for households already receiving them: nobody the plan makes newly entitled starts claiming, which understates those offsets and so overstates the net saving.

Concentration diagnostics remain private until support checks show at least ten contributing records in each reported total and each recoverable complement. Selecting ten records alone does not establish that ten records have nonzero contributions.

Every rule follows the triple lock to April 2029. The adjusted Triple Lock from April 2030 rises by at least the higher of CPI and 2.5% and by whatever else keeps the pension at its 2029-30 ratio to earnings, as DWP defines it; its top-up to the earnings path is rounded up to 0.1 point.

Only the basic and new State Pension change between the rules. Under both, the additional State Pension rises with September CPI and the Pension Credit guarantee with May-July earnings (the statutory minimum), and the State Pension age follows the law's timetable by date of birth, so every age of 67 and over is above it from 2028-29. There is no behavioural response.
Reported State Pension below State Pension age is not counted, as none is payable before it; every run records how many survey records report one (state_pension_accounting).
policyengine-uk 2.151.0 has no 25p State Pension age addition at 80 (#2340 is unmerged).

The binding primary is the UK Budget pair d2011 certifies (microcosm#1396): Microcosm national cut microcosm-uk-2024-25-national-20261025T091414Z-a6299504, policyengine-uk 2.151.0 and policyengine-core 3.33.3, certified by its policyengine.py 6.11.1 release (policyengine.py#720); publication fails closed without exactly that installed bundle. This scenarios-only build runs no paired sensitivity, so Enhanced FRS 1.58.2 gives only the data check. This model has September-CPI benefit uprating (#2557) but predates linked HB/Savings Credit derivation (#2576): the Savings Credit thresholds and pension-age HB allowances retain the installed lagged calendar-CPI projection (d1753); the Pension Credit guarantee still follows May-July earnings.
Costs are in cash terms (nominal £) for the UK; DWP's figures are for Great Britain. Each path run in the results file also gives its saving for Great Britain.

The OBR publishes no May-July earnings forecast, so the Pension Credit guarantee's rises from April 2028 to April 2031 follow its April-June average earnings growth, the same proxy the triple lock's earnings leg uses (3.3% in 2027, for April 2028). On the central path September CPI (3.4%) sets April 2028's State Pension rise, so a lower May-July figure would make the guarantee's April 2028 rise smaller and leave the pension's unchanged.

The pre-Budget release used Enhanced FRS and was described as provisional in Vahid's post. The binding release uses Microcosm; bridge step (b), on the same policyengine-uk 2.151.0 model, measures that change of data.

assumptions.title: Today's pensioners, reweighted to the ONS projection
assumptions.text: Each record keeps its survey age in every year to 2039-40. Each person's State Pension type follows their cohort: basic if they reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016, new otherwise. Household weights are raked each year to the ONS population projection by age and sex, so the number of pensioners follows it. DWP's costing projects the population; ours reweights the survey rather than ageing it.

benchmarks.title: State Pension uprating analysis 2026
benchmarks.figure_text: "-£15 billion" in "2039 to 2040" (Table 1: "In-year AME savings (nominal terms, rounded to nearest billion, negative values denote savings)"); "-£11 billion" in "real terms, 2025 to 2026 prices" (Table 2)
benchmarks.comparison: The adjusted Triple Lock vs the triple lock: State Pension spending in 2039-40, nominal, Great Britain; direct effects on AME only, no tax or debt interest
benchmarks.note: DWP estimates annual nominal Great Britain direct AME savings using Pensim3, rounded to £1bn, excluding tax and debt-interest effects; it applies a path for uprating that it does not publish. Ours is the gross saving in Great Britain in 2039-40 on the OBR's central path: one scenario, not an expected value, since the binding C2 score withdrew that. The two do not allow a like-for-like comparison; see HL3774 (answered 15 October 2026), https://questions-statements.parliament.uk/written-questions/detail/2026-10-05/hl3774.

benchmarks.title: Budget 2026
benchmarks.figure_text: "Adjusting the Triple Lock is estimated to reduce State Pension spending by £15 billion a year by the late 2030s, and by £50 billion a year by the late 2040s" (paragraph 1.29, chapter 1; its footnote 61 cites DWP, "State Pension Uprating", October 2026)
benchmarks.comparison: The adjusted Triple Lock vs the triple lock: State Pension spending by the late 2030s, the government's own figure, from DWP's analysis
benchmarks.note: The Budget takes its figures from DWP's uprating analysis: Great Britain, nominal, direct AME, for 2039-40 and 2049-50. Ours is the gross saving in Great Britain in 2039-40 on the OBR's central path, one scenario. The £50 billion falls after our horizon, which ends in 2039-40, so nothing here compares with it. Neither the OBR's October 2026 forecast (its policy table 1.1) nor the Treasury's policy costings and Table 6.1 itemise a costing of the adjustment.

benchmarks.title: Economic and fiscal outlook - October 2026
benchmarks.figure_text: "in our current medium-term forecast an uprating of 2.5 per cent would apply under both the previous and adjusted version of the triple lock in both 2030-31 and 2031-32" (paragraph 3.50, footnote 17)
benchmarks.comparison: The State Pension's rise in April 2030 (2030-31) under the adjusted Triple Lock, on the OBR's October 2026 medium-term forecast
benchmarks.note: The OBR has incorporated the adjusted Triple Lock into its forecast from 2030-31, where it changes no State Pension cost because both rules pay 2.5% in 2030-31 and 2031-32. Ours is the rise the central path pays under the adjusted Triple Lock in April 2030; its statutory inputs to 2030 are the same forecast's quarterly CPI and earnings.

benchmarks.title: Economic and fiscal outlook - October 2026
benchmarks.figure_text: "Averaging over the period as a whole, state pension payments would have been on average 1.4 per cent lower each year than under the current triple lock and 4.4 per cent higher than under earnings uprating" (paragraph 3.51, Chart 3.4: outturn earnings and inflation, 1990 to 2025, pension values from 1990)
benchmarks.comparison: The adjusted Triple Lock against the triple lock, replayed on outturn earnings and prices
benchmarks.note: The OBR averages payments over 35 years of outturn from a 1990 start. Ours is the adjusted Triple Lock's flat rate over the triple lock's after the April 2026 rise, replayed on the published September CPI and May-July earnings (April 2022's earnings leg suspended, as in law) with the adjusted rule starting in April 2017: one decade, read at its end rather than averaged. The OBR adds (paragraph 3.52) that the adjustment would reduce the projected long-term rise in debt by around 25% of GDP in 2075-76, beyond any horizon here.

benchmarks.title: Fiscal risks and sustainability - July 2025
benchmarks.figure_text: "we estimate that uprating by the triple lock rather than earnings will have added £15.5 billion (0.5 per cent of GDP) to state pension spending annually by 2029-30. This is around three times higher than the £5.2 billion we estimate the triple lock would have cost by that point under initial assumptions"
benchmarks.comparison: Triple lock vs earnings uprating since its introduction in April 2012: extra State Pension spending in 2029-30; the £5.2bn is that cost on the assumptions of the original 2010 costing and its long-run expectation of rises 0.2 points a year above earnings
benchmarks.note: OBR compares the triple lock with earnings uprating since 2012, in 2029-30. Ours is the gross saving in 2026-27 had the adjusted Triple Lock, which keeps the higher of CPI and 2.5% as a floor, started in April 2012.

benchmarks.title: What a ratchet! (Curtice and Clegg)
benchmarks.figure_text: "The OBR estimates spending on the State Pension would have been £12.6 billion lower this year with earnings-linked uprating than it is set to be with triple lock uprating, which we estimate would be a net saving of around £9 billion when we take account of lower income tax receipts and higher means-tested benefit spending."
benchmarks.comparison: Triple lock vs earnings-linked uprating, State Pension spending "this year" (2026-27 when RF wrote): £12.6bn gross is the OBR's estimate, £9bn net of income tax and means-tested benefits is RF's
benchmarks.note: RF's summary describes the same £12.6bn as against "a smoothed earnings link since 2012"; the report's own text attributes it to the OBR, against earnings-linked uprating. Ours is the net saving in 2026-27 had the adjusted Triple Lock (which keeps a CPI and 2.5% floor) started in April 2012.

benchmarks.title: Fiscal risks and sustainability - July 2026
benchmarks.figure_text: State pension spending, "which is projected to rise from 5 per cent of GDP to around 9 per cent of GDP over the projection period in the baseline. This is driven by population ageing and the cost of triple-lock uprating (calculated based on historical inflation and earnings volatility). In a scenario where the state pension is instead uprated in line with average earnings, state pension spending reaches around 7 per cent of GDP."
benchmarks.comparison: Triple lock vs earnings uprating over the 50-year projection to 2075-76, with the triple lock's cost calibrated to historical inflation and earnings volatility, % of GDP
benchmarks.note: A 50-year horizon in % of GDP with ageing; ours is in £bn for 2039-40 with survey ages held fixed, on the OBR-wedge scenario: the central path with the triple lock paying, from April 2032, the 'Triple lock' row of the OBR's March 2026 long-term determinants (average earnings growth plus 0.6 points beyond 2030-31), the OBR's own allowance for how often CPI or the floor beats earnings. One scenario, not an expected value.
